task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		Your phone has been showing 'No Service' for the past few hours.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You will consider the issue resolved when the status bar shows that you have signal. Always check the status bar if the agent asks you for status information. If the agent asks you to pay a bill, you accept. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

turns.thought:

**What you need to do next:**

turns.thought:
Totally understandable to ask — and no, a reboot will not erase your photos or anything else on your phone.

A "reboot" is just powering the phone completely off and then back on. Think of it like closing and reopening a program on a computer — your photos, contacts, and apps are all stored in the phone's memory and stay exactly where they are. Nothing gets deleted. It simply refreshes the phone's connection to the network so it can pick up your restored service.

Here's how to do it:
1. Press and hold the power button until you see a "Power off" or "Slide to power off" option on the screen.
2. Choose **Power off** and let the screen go completely dark.
3. Wait about 20–30 seconds.
4. Press and hold the power button again until the phone turns back on.

Once it's back on, look at the top of your screen — you should see signal bars and the network indicator (like 5G or LTE) instead of "No Service."

Take your time, and let me know once it's back on — I'll be right here to check whether your service is restored.
turns.execution_output: User: Well, alright. You're sure the pictures will be safe? Okay... I'll trust you. Let me turn it off and back on. Here goes.

turns.thought:
No, you didn't do anything wrong — and this is actually an easy fix! Airplane Mode just got turned on somehow while the phone was rebooting (it's easy to switch on by accident). That setting turns off all the wireless connections, which is why you see no signal bars.

No photos or data are affected — this is purely a connection setting, and nothing has been erased.

**Here's how to turn Airplane Mode off:**

On most phones, swipe down from the very top of the screen (like you're pulling down a shade). You'll see a row of quick-setting icons — look for the **airplane icon**. It's probably highlighted or lit up (blue/green/white) because it's on. Just **tap it once** so it goes gray or turns off.

A couple of notes:
- If you don't see it right away, swipe down once more to expand the full list of icons — the airplane one might be on a second page.
- On some phones it's under **Settings → Network & Internet** (or **Connections**), where you'd move the Airplane Mode slider to Off.

Once you tap it off, give the phone about 10–30 seconds. You should then see the signal bars and network indicator (like 5G or LTE) appear at the top instead of the airplane symbol.

Take your time with it, and let me know what you see at the top of the screen once you've done that.
turns.execution_output: User: Alright, let me try to turn that airplane thing off. I'll swipe down from the top like you said... okay, I think I found it. Let me tap it.

turns.thought:
I'm sorry this has been frustrating — you've done everything right, and the line itself is confirmed **Active** on our end now, so we just need to get your phone's settings straightened out. Two things are showing up, and they're both easy to fix:

**1. "Data Disabled" — turn mobile data back ON**

Swipe down from the top of the screen again to open those quick settings, and look for the **Mobile Data** icon (it often looks like two little up/down arrows, or says "Mobile Data" / "Cellular Data"). Tap it so it turns on/highlights.

**2. "No Signal" — let's check the SIM card**

Since your line is active and Airplane Mode is off, the most likely remaining cause is the SIM card (the small card inside the phone that connects you to the network) not being read properly. This happens sometimes, and it's nothing to worry about — it doesn't affect your photos.

If you're comfortable doing so:
- Power the phone **off** again.
- Locate the small tray on the edge of the phone (there's usually a tiny pinhole next to it — a paperclip or the SIM tool that came with the phone works to pop it open).
- Gently slide the tray out, check the little card is sitting flat and snug in the tray, then slide it back in firmly.
- Power the phone back on.

**If you'd rather not open up the phone — that's completely fine.** I can give you some other things to try first, or I can arrange for you to come into a store where someone can do it for you in person.

Try the mobile data step first, then let me know what the top of your screen says. And please don't worry — your photos are safe through all of this. Nothing we're doing touches what's stored on your phone.

turns.thought:
Absolutely — we don't need to touch the SIM card. Your photos are stored in the phone's own memory, not on the SIM, so they're safe either way, and I don't want you doing anything you're uncomfortable with.

First, let me reassure you about one thing: I re-checked your line on our end, and everything looks correct now —
- Line status: **Active** ✅
- Bill: **Paid** ✅
- Contract: valid through 2026-12-31 ✅
- Data usage: 8.7 GB of your 15 GB plan, so you're not out of data ✅

So this is a phone-side setting, not an account problem. Here are two safe things to try that don't involve opening anything:

**1. Reboot one more time (this often clears a stuck "Data Disabled" flag)**
Now that Airplane Mode is off and Mobile Data is on, power the phone all the way off again, wait about 30 seconds, and turn it back on. Sometimes the phone doesn't re-check the network until it restarts. This is the same safe restart you already did — nothing is erased.

**2. Check the network mode setting**
Open **Settings**, then look for **Network & Internet** (or **Connections**) → **Mobile Network** → **Network Mode** (it may be called "Preferred network type"). If it's set to **2G** or **3G**, change it to **4G/5G (recommended)** or "4G/5G auto." Older settings like 2G often can't find a signal on today's networks and can also block data and picture messaging.

Just take it one step at a time — do the reboot first, wait about a minute, and tell me exactly what the top of the screen says. No rush.

And if it's still showing "No Signal" after that, I will connect you with our technical support specialists who can run hands-on checks with you, or I can help you arrange an in-store appointment so someone can look at it in person. You shouldn't have to keep troubleshooting this yourself after everything you've already done — that's what we're here for.
